payload.stem: A closed rectangular loop carrying a steady current is placed in a uniform magnetic field with its plane at an angle to the field. Which statement about the net magnetic force and torque on the loop is correct and best justified?

options.text: The net magnetic force on the loop is zero, because the forces on opposite sides of the loop are equal and opposite in a uniform field, although the loop experiences a torque.
options.why: $\oint I\,d\vec l\times\vec B=I\left(\oint d\vec l\right)\times\vec B=0$ for a closed loop in a uniform field, while the forces on opposite sides act along different lines and produce a torque.

options.text: The net magnetic force on the loop is not zero, because the force on each side is nonzero and the forces add.
options.why: Adds the magnitudes of the side forces and ignores their directions.

options.text: The net magnetic force on the loop is zero and so is the net torque, because the forces cancel in every respect.
options.why: Believes that zero net force implies zero torque.

options.text: The net magnetic force on the loop is zero only if the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field, because otherwise no side feels a force.

options.text: The magnet falls just as fast as a nonmagnetic object, because copper is not magnetic and is not attracted by the magnet.

options.text: The magnet falls faster than a nonmagnetic object, because the induced currents attract it downward toward the tube.
options.why: Believes the induced currents attract the magnet instead of opposing its motion.

options.text: The magnet falls at constant speed from the start, because the induced currents exactly cancel gravity at every instant.
options.why: Believes the induced force is equal to the weight from the very start of the fall.

payload.title: Inserting a dielectric into a charged, isolated capacitor

stimulus.description: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor has square plates of area $A=200\text{ cm}^{2}$ separated by $d=4\text{ mm}$. It is charged by a $12\text{ V}$ battery and the battery is then disconnected. A dielectric slab of constant $\kappa=3$ that completely fills the gap is then inserted. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$ and $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ F/m}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the diagram of the capacitor in cross-section (two parallel plates, the top plate positive), draw several electric field lines in the gap before the dielectric is inserted, and mark the direction of the field. Then state how the density of the field lines in the gap should change after the dielectric is inserted.
parts.model_answer: Straight, evenly spaced field lines from the positive plate to the negative plate, perpendicular to the plates and pointing downward; after insertion the field in the gap is weaker (fewer lines per area) because the charge on the plates is unchanged.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws parallel field lines perpendicular to the plates, evenly spaced
common_errors: draws curved lines in the middle of the gap

rubric_rows.criterion: Marks the direction from the positive plate to the negative plate (downward)
common_errors: draws the arrows toward the positive plate

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the field in the gap becomes weaker (lines less dense) after the dielectric is inserted
common_errors: states that the field becomes stronger

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the capacitance $C$ with the dielectric in place and for the energy $U$ stored in the capacitor after the battery is disconnected and the dielectric inserted, in terms of $\kappa$, $\varepsilon_0$, $A$, $d$ and the initial voltage $V_0$.
parts.model_answer: $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$; the charge $Q=C_0V_0=\varepsilon_0AV_0/d$ is unchanged, so $U=Q^2/(2C)=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV_0^2}{2\kappa d}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ with the dielectric
common_errors: divides by $\kappa$

rubric_rows.criterion: Notes that the charge is unchanged, $Q=C_0V_0$ with $C_0=\varepsilon_0A/d$
common_errors: keeps the voltage fixed

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $U=Q^2/(2C)=\varepsilon_0AV_0^2/(2\kappa d)$
common_errors: obtains $\kappa\varepsilon_0AV_0^2/(2d)$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance with the dielectric in place and the energy stored after the insertion.
parts.model_answer: $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d\approx133\text{ pF}$ and $U=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV_0^2}{2\kappa d}\approx1.06\text{ nJ}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $C$ of about 133 with units of picofarads (accept any value within 2 percent)
common_errors: leaves the area in square centimeters

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $U$ of about 1.06 with units of nanojoules

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: How does the electric field in the gap after the insertion compare with the field before it? Calculate the ratio and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The field is reduced to $1/\kappa=0.333$ of its original value (from $3000\text{ V/m}$ to $1000\text{ V/m}$), because the free charge on the plates is unchanged while the dielectric's induced charge partly cancels the field.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the field is smaller by the factor $1/\kappa$ (about 0.333)
common_errors: states that the field is unchanged because the charge is unchanged
states that the field is multiplied by $\kappa$

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $E=\sigma/(\kappa\varepsilon_0)$ at fixed free charge density, or with $E=V/d$ and $V=Q/C$ falling by $\kappa$

payload.title: Inserting a dielectric into a charged, isolated capacitor

stimulus.description: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor has square plates of area $A=200\text{ cm}^{2}$ separated by $d=1\text{ mm}$. It is charged by a $50\text{ V}$ battery and the battery is then disconnected. A dielectric slab of constant $\kappa=3$ that completely fills the gap is then inserted. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$ and $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ F/m}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the diagram of the capacitor in cross-section (two parallel plates, the top plate positive), draw several electric field lines in the gap before the dielectric is inserted, and mark the direction of the field. Then state how the density of the field lines in the gap should change after the dielectric is inserted.
parts.model_answer: Straight, evenly spaced field lines from the positive plate to the negative plate, perpendicular to the plates and pointing downward; after insertion the field in the gap is weaker (fewer lines per area) because the charge on the plates is unchanged.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws parallel field lines perpendicular to the plates, evenly spaced
common_errors: draws curved lines in the middle of the gap

rubric_rows.criterion: Marks the direction from the positive plate to the negative plate (downward)
common_errors: draws the arrows toward the positive plate

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the field in the gap becomes weaker (lines less dense) after the dielectric is inserted
common_errors: states that the field becomes stronger

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the capacitance $C$ with the dielectric in place and for the energy $U$ stored in the capacitor after the battery is disconnected and the dielectric inserted, in terms of $\kappa$, $\varepsilon_0$, $A$, $d$ and the initial voltage $V_0$.
parts.model_answer: $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$; the charge $Q=C_0V_0=\varepsilon_0AV_0/d$ is unchanged, so $U=Q^2/(2C)=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV_0^2}{2\kappa d}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ with the dielectric
common_errors: divides by $\kappa$

rubric_rows.criterion: Notes that the charge is unchanged, $Q=C_0V_0$ with $C_0=\varepsilon_0A/d$
common_errors: keeps the voltage fixed

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $U=Q^2/(2C)=\varepsilon_0AV_0^2/(2\kappa d)$
common_errors: obtains $\kappa\varepsilon_0AV_0^2/(2d)$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance with the dielectric in place and the energy stored after the insertion.
parts.model_answer: $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d\approx531\text{ pF}$ and $U=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0AV_0^2}{2\kappa d}\approx73.75\text{ nJ}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $C$ of about 531 with units of picofarads (accept any value within 2 percent)
common_errors: leaves the area in square centimeters

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $U$ of about 73.75 with units of nanojoules

parts.prompt: How does the electric field in the gap after the insertion compare with the field before it? Calculate the ratio and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The field is reduced to $1/\kappa=0.333$ of its original value (from $50000\text{ V/m}$ to $16667\text{ V/m}$), because the free charge on the plates is unchanged while the dielectric's induced charge partly cancels the field.

states that the field is multiplied by $\kappa$

common_errors: argues only that the dielectric blocks the field without a quantitative relation

payload.title: Potential on the axis of a charged ring

stimulus.description: A thin ring of radius $R=20\text{ cm}$ carries a uniform charge $Q=6\text{ nC}$ and lies in the plane $x=0$ with its center at the origin, so the $x$-axis is its axis. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the electric potential $V$ on the axis as a function of $x$ for $-3R\le x\le3R$ (zero potential at infinity). Label the value of the potential at $x=0$ and at $x=R$ in terms of $k$, $Q$ and $R$.
parts.model_answer: A symmetric bell-shaped curve with its maximum $kQ/R$ at $x=0$, falling to $kQ/(\sqrt2R)$ at $x=\pm R$ and approaching zero for large $|x|$, always positive.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units
The curve is symmetric about $x=0$ with its maximum at the origin, labeled $kQ/R$
common_errors: draws a minimum at the origin

rubric_rows.criterion: Labels the value $kQ/(\sqrt2R)$ at $x=\pm R$
common_errors: labels $kQ/(2R)$

rubric_rows.criterion: The curve stays positive and approaches zero at large $|x|$
common_errors: draws a curve that crosses zero

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the electric potential at a point on the axis a distance $x$ from the center in terms of $k$, $Q$, $R$ and $x$.
parts.model_answer: Every element of charge $dq$ is the same distance $\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$ from the point, so $V=\int\dfrac{k\,dq}{\sqrt{x^2+R^2}}=\dfrac{kQ}{\sqrt{x^2+R^2}}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the potential of a charge element, $dV=k\,dq/\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$
common_errors: uses $k\,dq/(x^2+R^2)$

rubric_rows.criterion: Recognizes that the distance is the same for all elements, so the integral is just $\int dq=Q$
required_elements: same distance, integral of dq equals Q
common_errors: inserts an angle dependence

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $V=kQ/\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$
common_errors: obtains $kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Use the potential to find the magnitude of the electric field on the axis at $x=R$, and calculate its value.
parts.model_answer: $E_x=-dV/dx=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$, which at $x=R$ is $kQ/(2^{3/2}R^2)\approx477\text{ N/C}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $E_x=-dV/dx$ and differentiates $V$
common_errors: integrates instead of differentiating

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $E_x=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$
common_errors: omits the factor $x$ in the numerator

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the field at $x=R$ of about 477 with units of newtons per coulomb (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A charged ring of twice the radius and the same total charge is used. By what factor does the potential at the center change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The potential at the center is $kQ/R$, so doubling the radius at fixed charge halves it (from $270\text{ V}$ to $135\text{ V}$), because every charge element is twice as far from the center.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the potential at the center is halved (factor 0.5)
common_errors: states that it is quartered
states that it is unchanged because the charge is the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $V=kQ/R$ at the center (proportional to $1/R$ at fixed $Q$)
common_errors: argues with the $1/r^2$ field law

difficulty.label: basic_learning
difficulty.rationale: Standard core application of F = qv x B. Part A requires recognizing that the force is perpendicular to velocity and does no work, so KE is constant. Part B is a routine derivation (qvB = mv^2/r, r = mv/(eB)) with a single plug-in giving about 4.2 cm. Part C is a simple 1/B proportional prediction (radius halves). Each part is one governing law with few steps, low reading load, and clean numbers. No difficulty comes from unfair sources.
